ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, a wooden block weighing 40 N is initially at rest on a horizontal table. At a certain moment, it is simultaneously subjected to two opposite horizontal forces $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$, where $F_{1}=13\mathrm{N}$ and $F_{2}=6\mathrm{N}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the ground is 0.2, and it is assumed that the maximum static friction equals the sliding friction.

1. The magnitude and direction of the frictional force acting on the wooden block.
2. When only $F_{1}$ is removed, the magnitude and direction of the frictional force acting on the block.
3. If the force removed is not $F_{1}$ but $F_{2}$, find the magnitude and direction of the frictional force acting on the block.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
$7\mathrm{N}$, direction to the left
$6\mathrm{N}$, direction to the right
$8\mathrm{N}$, direction to the left

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached diagram shows a wooden block on a horizontal rough table. A horizontal force F1 is drawn on the left side with its arrow pointing to the right toward the block. A horizontal force F2 is drawn on the right side with its arrow pointing to the left toward the block. Thus F1 acts rightward and F2 acts leftward. Reasoning: The block weighs 40 N, so on the horizontal table the normal force is N = 40 N. The kinetic friction is μN = 0.2 × 40 = 8 N, and the problem states the maximum static friction equals this value, so f_s,max = 8 N. 1. With both forces present, the applied-force resultant excluding friction is 13 N right − 6 N left = 7 N right. Since 7 N < 8 N, static friction can balance it. Therefore the block remains at rest and friction is 7 N to the left. 2. If only F1 is removed, only F2 = 6 N left remains. Since 6 N < 8 N, static friction balances it. Therefore friction is 6 N to the right. 3. If instead F2 is removed, only F1 = 13 N right remains. Since 13 N > 8 N, static friction cannot hold the block; it moves right. The friction is then sliding friction of magnitude 8 N, opposite the motion, so it is to the left.

raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: The attached diagram shows a wooden block on a horizontal rough table. A horizontal force F1 is drawn on the left side with its arrow pointing to the right toward the block. A horizontal force F2 is drawn on the right side with its arrow pointing to the left toward the block. Thus F1 acts rightward and F2 acts leftward.

Reasoning: The block weighs 40 N, so on the horizontal table the normal force is N = 40 N. The kinetic friction is μN = 0.2 × 40 = 8 N, and the problem states the maximum static friction equals this value, so f_s,max = 8 N.

1. With both forces present, the applied-force resultant excluding friction is 13 N right − 6 N left = 7 N right. Since 7 N < 8 N, static friction can balance it. Therefore the block remains at rest and friction is 7 N to the left.

2. If only F1 is removed, only F2 = 6 N left remains. Since 6 N < 8 N, static friction balances it. Therefore friction is 6 N to the right.

3. If instead F2 is removed, only F1 = 13 N right remains. Since 13 N > 8 N, static friction cannot hold the block; it moves right. The friction is then sliding friction of magnitude 8 N, opposite the motion, so it is to the left.
